summary: Lists requirements for Path Computation Clients and Path Computation Elements to support point-to-multipoint MPLS-TE paths. PCEs compute paths for traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A map-planning helper must learn to plan routes with one start and many ends, and this lists what it needs.

questions: what is a pce in mpls
subtitle: What a path computation protocol must add so a PCE can plan one-to-many MPLS traffic-engineered paths.

tldr.problem: Computing routes for point-to-multipoint (P2MP) traffic-engineered paths is hard, and the generic PCC-PCE requirements in RFC 4657 do not cover trees with many destinations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 15 numbered requirements (R1 to R15) for the PCC-PCE protocol, such as an explicit P2MP indication, multiple destinations, tree-shaped replies, multi-message exchanges and branch-node controls.
tldr.outcome: It adds parameters to existing messages rather than new messages, and complements the generic requirements. It is a requirements document, not a protocol.

today: RFC 5862 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for the PCC-PCE protocol as of June 2010 and is not itself a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why P2MP Needs Extra Requirements
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes network paths from a network graph and constraints. It is intended for traffic engineered Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs) in MPLS and GMPLS networks. A Path Computation Client (PCC) is the party that asks.

Path computation for point-to-multipoint TE LSPs is a significant challenge, and optimizing several of them takes considerable computing resources, so PCE offers a way to offload that work from Label Switching Routers. The RFC supplements the generic requirements in RFC 4657, and does not justify the use of PCE for P2MP, which is covered in a companion document, RFC 5671.
sections.eli5: Planning a road from one town to one town is easy. Planning a delivery tree from one warehouse to many shops is harder, so the planner needs more instructions.

sections.title: Requests, Destinations and Replies
sections.content:
No new messages are needed. The existing PCC-PCE messages gain parameters for P2MP.

  • R1: an explicit parameter in a conspicuous place SHOULD mark a request as P2MP.
  • R3: a PCE MUST be able to reject a P2MP request with a reason code meaning no support.
  • R4: at least one required P2MP parameter MUST cause an unmodified back-level PCE to reject the request as unprocessable or unrecognized.
  • R5: one request MUST be able to list multiple destinations.
  • R6 and R7: the reply MUST carry the P2MP path, either compressed or as a set of source-to-leaf (S2L) sub-paths, and SHOULD use the compressed format by default.
  • R8: a request or response MUST be able to span a sequence of messages when the tree is too large for one.
  • R9: different constraints or quality-of-service settings for different destinations of one LSP MUST NOT be possible.
sections.eli5: The request must say clearly that it wants a tree, may list many destinations, and a planner that cannot do trees must be able to say so. Big answers can come in several pieces.

sections.title: Changes, Reoptimization and Diversity
sections.content:
For existing trees, R10 says a request MUST be able to carry an existing path, and that path MUST be allowed to be P2MP, compressed or not. R11 requires reoptimization of P2MP TE LSPs. Because re-signaling any LSP risks stability even with make-before-break, a request SHOULD carry a cost-benefit reoptimization threshold for the whole LSP and per destination, and replies SHOULD indicate which routes changed.

R12 covers adding or removing leaves. A request MUST be able to carry the existing tree, say which destinations are new, and say which existing destinations must not have their paths modified. R13 lets a PCC specify a limiting set of allowed branch nodes and a list of nodes that must not be branch nodes. R15 says a PCC SHOULD be able to ask for a secondary tree with partial path diversity for specific leaves or an S2L sub-path.
sections.eli5: When a shop is added or closed, you should be able to say what to leave alone, which crossroads may be used as splitting points, and how much improvement is worth redoing the whole plan.

sections.title: Capabilities and Manageability
sections.content:
R2 keeps the requirement to specify objective functions, but notes that new ones will be needed for P2MP and defined in a separate document. R14 says P2MP ability and supported objective functions SHOULD be advertised in PCE discovery; if not, the protocol MUST let a PCC discover them.

On manageability, a PCE MAY have a switch to enable or disable P2MP support and MAY hide its P2MP capabilities from certain PCCs by policy, or refuse requests for any reason. Protocol extensions SHOULD come with MIB objects. Liveness detection should account for P2MP computations being likely to take longer than P2P ones, and the topology graph must include the P2MP signaling and branching capabilities of each LSR. Adding P2MP to a PCE may significantly change its load, especially during recovery after a network failure.
sections.eli5: Planners should announce whether they can do trees, an operator should be able to switch that on and off, and everyone should expect tree planning to take longer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: P2MP computation requests raise no additional security issues, since there are no new messages and no new PCC-PCE relationships or transactions. They are, however, more CPU-intensive and use more link bandwidth. If the protocol were susceptible to denial of service by spurious requests, P2MP support would make the effect worse. The RFC says it would be possible to apply different authorization policies to P2MP requests.
sections.eli5: Tree requests cost the planner more effort, so a prankster sending fake requests could cause more trouble. Special rules for who may ask for trees could help.
